title: Surface-switchable nonreciprocity protected by Fermi arcs in Weyl semimetal TaAs
authors: Dong Li, Yuki M. Itahashi, Ying-Ming Xie, Menghu Zhou, Yukako Fujishiro, Kunjie Zheng, Yao Guang, Max T. Birch, Ilya Belopolski, Max Hirschberger, Takahiro Morimoto, Xiao-Xiao Zhang, Zhi-An Ren, Naoto Nagaosa, Yoshihiro Iwasa
abstract: Weyl semimetals host topologically protected surface states, known as Fermi arcs, which connect bulk Weyl nodes in momentum space. Both bulk Weyl nodes and Fermi arcs are anticipated to be chiral. The chirality of bulk bands has been confirmed through observations of the chiral anomaly and Weyl orbits. In contrast, despite their discovery more than a decade ago, the chiral nature of Fermi arcs has remained unresolved. Here we report Fermi-arc-induced nonlinear transport in the archetypal Weyl semimetal TaAs. Using focused ion beam techniques, we fabricated micro-scale devices that enable simultaneous transport measurements on opposing topological surfaces. While linear transport remains dominated by bulk conduction, nonlinear transport uncovers surface-specific contributions, including an exceptionally large third-order nonreciprocal response that exceeds conventional expectations and highlights the crucial role of the singular arc endpoints. Our findings unambiguously demonstrate the chiral nature of Fermi arcs and establish nonlinear transport as a direct probe of these topological surface states. By revealing a surface-switchable, room-temperature nonlinear response that is topologically protected, this work introduces a new functionality in Weyl semimetals. Given the abundance of natural materials predicted to host topological semimetal states, these results open opportunities for exploring nonlinear transport phenomena and device concepts across a broad class of systems.
summary: The research reports on measuring nonreciprocal second-harmonic resistance ($R_{2\omega}$) in the Weyl semimetal $	ext{TaAs}$ to prove the existence and chirality of Fermi arcs. By comparing measurements on opposing surfaces, they observed a robust sign reversal and higher-order angular modulations that are absent in bulk conduction, establishing nonlinear transport as a direct probe for these topological surface states.
main_problem: To experimentally resolve the chiral nature of Fermi arcs—topologically protected surface states in Weyl semimetals—by developing a nonlinear transport measurement technique.
main_result: The study unambiguously demonstrates the chiral nature of Fermi arcs through observing a surface-switchable, sign-reversed, and higher-order nonreciprocal second-harmonic response ($R_{2\omega}$) that is robust up to room temperature.
method: Fabrication of micro-scale devices using Focused Ion Beam (FIB) techniques followed by nonlinear AC transport measurements ($R_{2\omega}$) on opposing topological surfaces.
model_or_system: The physical system is the archetypal Weyl semimetal, Tantalum Arsenide ($	ext{TaAs}$), which hosts topologically protected surface states known as Fermi arcs connecting bulk Weyl nodes in momentum space.
key_observables: Second-harmonic magnetoresistance ($R_{2\omega}$), exhibiting sign reversal between top and bottom surfaces, and angular modulations fitting $\sin(	heta)$ and $\sin(3	heta)$.
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, magnetic field strength (up to 8.9 T), current density ($J$), and surface orientation (top vs. bottom).
main_assumptions: Linear transport measurements are dominated by bulk conduction, while the nonlinear response is uniquely sensitive to the topological surface states; theoretical models based on Boltzmann transport fail quantitatively.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the magnetic field dependence of $R_{2\omega}$ showing opposite signs for top/bottom surfaces (Fig 2a), current and angular dependencies revealing $\sin(	heta)$ and $\sin(3	heta)$ patterns (Figs 2c, 4b, 4c), and thickness dependence confirming surface origin (Fig 3).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the need for a new probe (nonlinear transport) due to bulk dominance in linear measurements. It presents evidence of surface-specific signals via sign reversal, confirms topological protection through robustness across temperature/thickness, and finally uses higher-order angular modulations ($\sin(3	heta)$) as definitive 'smoking-gun' evidence.
why_interesting: This work provides a novel, highly sensitive, and topologically protected diagnostic tool for characterizing surface states in Weyl semimetals using nonlinear electrical transport, which is valuable for developing next-generation topological electronic devices.
